title: Front End and Back End
body: "Frontend" and "Backend" are terms that describe the division of roles in a web application.
when_to_show: When reviewing frontend, backend, api, web
detail: The frontend consists of the user interface—including screens, buttons, and input fields—while the backend handles tasks on the server, such as data storage, login, API processing, and validation. Although Python is primarily used for backend development, there are also structures—such as learning apps—where static JSON is read directly on the screen. When reviewing code, it becomes easier to understand if you can distinguish whether a file is intended for the user interface or for server-side processing.

title: HTML, CSS, JavaScript
body: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript are the three fundamental elements used to create web pages.
when_to_show: When reviewing html, css, javascript, web
detail: HTML defines the structure of the page, CSS determines its appearance—such as colors and sizes—and JavaScript handles actions like button clicks and data loading. In the Python learning app, data is stored in JSON format, and JavaScript reads that data on the screen to display it as cards. When reading web code, you must distinguish between structure, style, and behavior. These cards are not just for memorizing definitions; they serve as supplementary explanations to help you identify how variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are connected in actual Python code.

title: PWA: Using the Web Like an App
body: PWA stands for Progressive Web App, which is a way to make a website function like an app. Although it opens in a browser just like a regular web page, it can be added to the home screen, use an offline cache, and provide an app-like experience. In a learning app, for example, it receives a lesson JSON file and displays it on the screen, while a service worker can cache certain files. When reading the code, PWAs involve not only HTML, CSS, and JavaScript but also caching, versioning, and offline behavior. This card is not just for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary guide to help you identify which variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are involved in actual Python code. When solving problems, first locate the line in the code where this concept appears, then determine whether that line reads input, modifies a value, evaluates a condition, or stores or outputs a result.
when_to_show: Mobile Web App, GitHub Pages Issue
detail: A PWA is a method that allows users to install and use a website just like an app. It combines standard HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with a manifest, service workers, and a caching strategy to enable features such as adding the app to the home screen and offline usage. When reviewing the code, you should examine the app version, the files targeted for caching, and the update process following a new deployment.

title: GitHub Pages: Deploying a Static Site
body: GitHub Pages is a GitHub feature that allows you to deploy static websites.
detail: You can publish files—such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and JSON—that can be read directly in a browser without server-side code via a web address. If your Python learning app has a static PWA structure, you can deploy it on a platform like GitHub Pages. When reading code, you must distinguish whether it involves server-side processing or a structure where the browser reads pre-generated files. title: localStorage: Browser Storage
body: localStorage is a feature that stores small amounts of data within the browser. Even without a server, it allows you to save values such as user settings, the last card viewed, and simple progress status in the browser.
when_to_show: When reviewing localStorage, browser, memo, progress
detail: Since values are typically stored as strings, you must convert objects or lists to strings using `JSON.stringify` to store them, and then restore them using `JSON.parse` when reading them back. When reading the code, it’s important to distinguish that localStorage is a storage mechanism within the user’s browser, not a server database. This card is not just for memorizing word definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how these concepts—such as variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows—are connected in actual Python code.

title: CORS: Browser permission for cross-origin responses
body: An origin is the combination of scheme, host, and port; a difference in any one makes it a different origin in the browser. For front-end JavaScript to use an API response across origins, the server must authorize the relevant origin, HTTP method, and request headers through CORS response headers. For some requests the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight, while a simple request may reach the server but still be unreadable to JavaScript when the required response header is absent. That is why a request can appear in backend logs while the browser console reports a CORS error. CORS is a browser cross-origin policy, not a substitute for user authentication, API authorization, or a server firewall, and it does not block non-browser clients such as curl.
when_to_show: When connecting a browser front end to an API on a different origin
detail: Compare the schemes, hosts, and ports of the front-end and request URLs, then inspect the server's allowed origins, methods, headers, and actual CORS response headers. Distinguish a preflight failure from an API failure, and do not mistake CORS for authentication or access control.

title: Routing: Linking Addresses to Screens/Functions
body: Routing is a structure that links addresses to screens or functions. For example, when a user navigates to /home, the home screen is displayed, and when a request is made to /api/items, data is returned. Front-end routing changes the screen based on the URL, while back-end routing executes server functions based on the URL. Even in static PWAs, URLs, file paths, and screen states can be linked. When reading code, routing serves as a clue for tracking which code a user’s request triggers. This card is not meant merely for memorizing definitions; it is an explanatory aid to help you identify which variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are connected in actual Python code. When solving problems, first locate the line in the code where this concept appears, then determine whether that line reads input, modifies values, evaluates conditions, or stores or outputs results. Routing is a set of rules that connects URLs to screens or features. When reading web app code, you must verify which components or handlers the URLs the user navigates to correspond to, and how non-existent URLs are handled.
when_to_show: When reviewing routing, url, endpoint, spa
detail: Routing is a set of rules that maps URLs to screens or server functions. Front-end routing changes the screen state based on the URL, while back-end routing selects the function to execute based on the URL and HTTP method. When reading code, you should check the URL the user entered, the matching route, how unrecognized URLs are handled, and how API endpoints are distinguished.

title: Certification and Authorization
body: Authentication and authorization are common concepts in web service security. Authentication is the process of verifying a user’s identity, while authorization is the process of determining which features that user is permitted to use. Logging in is similar to authentication, whereas restricting access to a specific page to administrators only is similar to authorization. When reading code and encountering the term “auth,” you should also examine how tokens, sessions, permissions, and user IDs are handled. This card is not intended merely for memorizing definitions; rather, it serves as a supplementary guide to help you identify how these concepts relate to specific variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows in actual Python code. Authentication is the process of verifying who a user is, while authorization is the process of determining what that user is allowed to do. A successful login is authentication, whereas granting access to the admin dashboard is closer to authorization. When reading code, you must distinguish between the parts that validate tokens and those that check permissions. If you mix the two, it’s easy to overlook the security flow.
when_to_show: When reviewing auth, oauth, jwt, session
detail: Authentication is the process of verifying a user’s identity, while authorization is the process of determining what that user is permitted to do. A successful login does not automatically grant all permissions. When reading code, you should distinguish between the parts that validate tokens or sessions and those that check roles, permissions, and administrator status.

title: API Request
summary: An API request is an action in which client or server code calls a function on another server.
detail: An API request is an agreed-upon channel through which clients and servers exchange data. During code reviews, we examine everything from the URL, method, headers, query parameters, body payload, timeout, and status code to the handling of `response.json` and error handling. It’s important not only to verify whether the request was successful but also to see how failure responses and network exceptions are handled.
body: An API request is a request sent by a program to another program or server to obtain necessary information. Just as a person clicks a button in a web browser, Python code can also send requests to a server’s address and receive responses. For example, a weather app sends location information to a weather server, and the server returns data such as temperature and forecasts. In this process, requests may include a URL, parameters, and authentication information, while responses typically come in a structured format such as JSON. When reading code, you must identify where the request is being sent, what values are being sent, and which fields are being extracted from the response. APIs are a core concept in real-world development, connecting to input, dictionaries, JSON, exception handling, and security key management. When reviewing this card, don’t just memorize the definitions—also verify how they relate to specific variables, functions, and data types in actual code. The goal is to apply the concepts you’ve learned from these small examples to data processing and service architecture in real-world projects. An API request is the channel through which the front end and back end exchange data. The browser sends a request to the server, and the server responds with JSON or a status code. When reading code, you should check the request URL, method, headers, body, and the order of response handling. It’s also important to understand how failure responses and network errors are handled.
